paragraphs: Accelerated MR imaging collects fewer measurements to shorten acquisition time. The resulting reconstruction problem can admit many plausible images, so producing a single image leaves part of that ambiguity unexplored. This paper instead learns to sample from the posterior distribution: a distribution of possible images conditioned on the available measurements.

The proposed conditional normalizing flow targets the signal component in the measurement operator’s nullspace. This is the part of the signal that the measurements do not determine. The model infers that missing component and then combines it with measured data to construct complete images. This design ties the generative task directly to the structure of the reconstruction problem.

Experiments using fastMRI brain and knee data report fast inference and better accuracy than recent MRI posterior sampling techniques. The contribution therefore concerns both reconstruction performance and the ability to produce multiple plausible solutions. Such samples can provide downstream inference tasks with more comprehensive information than a single reconstruction, while the reported comparisons establish the method’s effectiveness on the evaluated data.
icml-2023-a-conditional-normalizing-flow.tldr: A conditional normalizing flow reconstructs accelerated MRI by sampling unmeasured signal components, producing plausible images with strong reported accuracy and fast inference.

paragraphs: Classification usually relies on a label for each training example, but obtaining those labels can be expensive or raise privacy concerns. Classification from aggregate observations uses information attached to groups instead. This setting includes multiple-instance learning and learning from label proportions, which provide different forms of group supervision.

The paper proposes a shared approach that weights the importance of each example and each possible label within its group. These weights turn aggregate information into supervision that a classifier can use. The central theoretical result is an unbiased estimate of classification risk that works with arbitrary loss functions, rather than requiring a particular loss to make the method valid.

An unbiased risk estimate targets the intended classification objective on average, and the authors establish risk consistency for their method. Experiments across several aggregate-supervision problems report advantages over compared approaches. Together, the results suggest that group labels can support a broadly applicable training strategy, with flexibility in the loss function and a theoretical connection to the classification risk being optimized.
icml-2023-a-universal-unbiased-method-fo.tldr: The paper turns group-level supervision into weighted training signals with an unbiased classification-risk estimator compatible with arbitrary losses.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning depends on augmented versions of graphs to learn useful representations without labels. Common augmentations randomly remove nodes or change edges. Those edits can damage meaningful structure and encourage a model to focus on background patterns that are less relevant to what distinguishes the graph.

The proposed framework uses gradient-based Graph Contrastive Saliency to identify graph substructures that matter to the contrastive learning objective. It then uses those saliency signals to create augmentations with more meaningful structural content. The approach makes augmentation adaptive: the learning process helps determine which parts of a graph deserve attention when generating training views.

The authors report empirical support across 16 benchmark datasets and provide theoretical justification for robustness properties of the saliency measure. The findings support treating augmentation design as part of learning, rather than relying entirely on random graph changes. The stated benefit is better generalization through attention to discriminative structure; the experiments demonstrate this benefit in the evaluated benchmark settings.
icml-2023-boosting-graph-contrastive-lea.tldr: Gradient-based graph saliency guides contrastive augmentations toward meaningful substructures, with theoretical robustness support and empirical benefits across 16 datasets.

paragraphs: Continual learning systems must learn new tasks while retaining earlier knowledge. Rehearsal methods address forgetting by keeping a small, fixed-size collection of past examples and revisiting them during learning. This paper argues that using those examples also calls for attention to relationships between tasks, including what should remain task-specific and what can be shared.

DualHSIC adds two complementary components built from the Hilbert Schmidt independence criterion. HSIC-Bottleneck for Rehearsal reduces interference between tasks, while HSIC Alignment encourages the sharing of task-invariant knowledge. These components address different pressures in continual learning: preserving useful distinctions and retaining knowledge that remains relevant across tasks.

The method is designed to augment existing rehearsal approaches. Extensive experiments report consistent improvements when it is added to those methods, including better performance than recent rehearsal methods enhanced with regularization. The results suggest that a memory buffer’s value depends partly on how learning organizes the relationships among its tasks, beyond simply retaining and replaying past data.
icml-2023-dualhsic-hsic-bottleneck-and-a.tldr: DualHSIC improves rehearsal-based continual learning by reducing interference between tasks and encouraging shared task-invariant knowledge.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning tasks require keeping the system out of specified unsafe regions. In an unknown, stochastic environment, this is difficult to enforce through a bound on expected cumulative violation costs. That cost-based formulation can be an indirect way of expressing the actual concern: the chance that the system reaches an unsafe state.

The paper uses barrier functions to encode safety chance constraints explicitly. Because the environment is unknown, it relaxes these functions into soft barriers based on a generative model. A bi-level optimization procedure then learns the environment and optimizes the control policy together, using safety probability as part of the optimization.

Experiments on a set of examples show effective enforcement of the safety chance constraints and substantially higher simulated safe rates than the compared constrained Markov decision process methods. These findings concern probabilistic safety in the evaluated stochastic settings. The approach matters because its learning objective is connected more directly to avoiding unsafe regions, rather than relying solely on accumulated violation costs.
icml-2023-enforcing-hard-constraints-wit.tldr: Soft barrier functions support joint environment and policy learning to enforce safety chance constraints, improving simulated safe rates over the evaluated CMDP methods.

paragraphs: Graph representations need enough detail to distinguish different graph structures, but richer representations can be expensive to compute. This paper studies random embeddings that balance these demands. Its target is a representation whose expressive power can grow as more resources become available, supporting the broader aim of approximating arbitrary functions on graphs.

The construction builds on a characterization of graph isomorphism using an infinite vector of homomorphism counts. These counts describe structure-preserving mappings between graphs. The proposed random embeddings can distinguish every pair of non-isomorphic graphs in expectation and can be computed in expected polynomial time. Both qualifications matter: the guarantees concern expectations, rather than requiring every individual random embedding to distinguish every graph.

Empirical evaluation finds competitive performance on several graph learning benchmarks. The theoretical contribution is a route toward increasingly expressive representations with an expected computational guarantee. The experiments complement that result by showing that the approach can also be useful on practical learning tasks, beyond its ability to separate graph structures in expectation.
icml-2023-expectation-complete-graph-rep.tldr: Random homomorphism-based embeddings distinguish all non-isomorphic graphs in expectation while remaining computable in expected polynomial time.

paragraphs: Some learning algorithms considered in neuroscience and neuromorphic computing learn by contrasting different sets of network states. Their standard implementations rely on rigid, periodic phases and information spanning separated moments in time. Those timing requirements may restrict which biological or physical systems could implement the learning process.

This paper investigates how much of that prescribed timing is actually needed. Building on work on biological and neuromorphic implementations, it shows that contrastive learning can be made temporally local and can continue functioning when many standard dynamical requirements are relaxed. Temporal locality addresses how learning can operate using information available locally in time.

The authors establish general theorems and support them with numerical experiments across several contrastive learning models. The contribution is a theoretical basis for exploring a wider range of learning dynamics in biological and neuromorphic networks. It shows flexibility in the timing of these algorithms without claiming that every possible physical implementation or arbitrary relaxation will preserve learning.
icml-2023-flexible-phase-dynamics-for-bi.tldr: The paper shows that several contrastive learning models can use temporally local learning and tolerate relaxed phase dynamics, supported by theory and numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Differential privacy composition tracks privacy loss across repeated interactions with data. Advanced composition provides stronger accounting than simply adding privacy costs, but standard results require fixing privacy parameters in advance. Fully adaptive composition allows both the algorithms and their privacy settings to depend on earlier interactions.

The paper improves two tools for this setting. Privacy filters provide differential privacy guarantees for the combined interaction, while privacy odometers bound accumulated privacy loss over time. The new filters match advanced composition rates, including constants, despite adaptive parameter choices. The authors also derive a filter for approximate zero-concentrated differential privacy.

The new families of odometers match advanced composition tightness at a chosen time, or provide simultaneous guarantees over time with a doubly logarithmic factor. The proofs use advances in martingale concentration. These results make the cost of adaptivity much smaller than earlier bounds suggested, while preserving the distinction between a guarantee at one preselected time and a bound that remains valid throughout an interaction.
icml-2023-fully-adaptive-composition-in-.tldr: New privacy filters and odometers bring fully adaptive differential privacy accounting close to the guarantees of advanced composition.

paragraphs: An optimization problem can have useful convexity in a curved geometry even when its ordinary Euclidean formulation looks different. This paper considers objectives that are geodesically convex and can also be expressed as the difference of two Euclidean convex functions. That combination appears in problems involving matrix scaling, scatter-matrix estimation, and Brascamp-Lieb inequalities.

The difference-of-convex structure lets the authors use the Euclidean Convex-Concave Procedure, or CCCP. This offers a way to avoid potentially expensive Riemannian operations while still exploiting the problem’s underlying geometry. The algorithmic opportunity comes from using one structure for computation and another for the convergence analysis.

Existing CCCP theory generally guarantees convergence to stationary points. By using overall geodesic convexity, the paper instead establishes iteration-complexity results for global optimality in the studied setting. Concrete optimization examples illustrate the results and yield competitive solvers. The stronger conclusion depends on this combined structure; it does not make arbitrary difference-of-convex problems globally solvable by CCCP.
icml-2023-global-optimality-for-euclidea.tldr: For geodesically convex objectives with a Euclidean difference-of-convex form, CCCP gains global-optimality complexity guarantees while avoiding potentially costly Riemannian operations.

paragraphs: This paper uses diffusion models for problems commonly approached with algorithms, including sorting, Sudoku constraint satisfaction, and matrix factorization. Its central question is how a generative model can benefit from knowing the structure of the problem it must solve. The proposed framework automatically defines and learns models with architectures tailored to that structure.

The problem specification must include a graphical model describing relationships among variables. Explicitly representing intermediate subcomputations can also help, and the framework can exploit permutation invariances when they apply. These ingredients provide architectural information about how parts of the problem relate and which changes in ordering should leave relevant behavior unchanged.

Across a diverse collection of experiments, the authors report better scaling of training time and final accuracy as problem dimension grows. The finding concerns how performance changes with problem size, making it particularly relevant to structured tasks that become harder at larger dimensions. The framework’s contribution is a systematic connection between a problem specification and the design of a learned generative solver.
icml-2023-graphically-structured-diffusi.tldr: Problem-specific graphical structure guides diffusion-model architectures, improving how training time and accuracy scale in the evaluated algorithmic tasks.

paragraphs: Repeated auction bidding requires balancing opportunities to win against a limited spending budget. This paper studies that problem for first-price auctions, motivated by changes in online advertising markets. The learning challenge depends partly on what a bidder can observe after each auction, since feedback determines what can be learned about competing bids.

The authors develop a dual-based algorithm for full-information feedback, where the maximum competing bid is revealed after every auction. They prove a near-optimal regret bound of roughly the square root of the number of auctions, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Regret measures the performance gap to the comparison benchmark, so this bound controls how that gap grows across repeated decisions.

They then modify the algorithm for one-sided feedback, where only the winning bid is disclosed. The same regret order remains achievable under mild assumptions on the bidder’s value distribution. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of the budget policy. The results connect budget management with learning under two feedback regimes, while retaining an explicit distributional condition for the less informative setting.
icml-2023-learning-to-bid-in-repeated-fi.tldr: A dual-based bidding algorithm achieves near-optimal regret under full feedback and the same regret order under one-sided feedback with mild value-distribution assumptions.

paragraphs: Neural predictions often need to obey constraints as well as fit data. LinSATNet studies how to incorporate positive linear satisfiability into neural networks through a differentiable layer. Differentiability allows the constraint-handling component to participate in training, making feasibility part of the network’s computation.

The layer extends the Sinkhorn algorithm to jointly encode multiple sets of marginal distributions. The paper derives the underlying formulation and theoretically characterizes convergence for this multiple-marginal setting. This provides both a computational construction and an analysis of the procedure used to impose the constraints.

The authors demonstrate one-shot neural solvers in three applications: routing learned without optimal-solution supervision, partial graph matching with unmatchable outliers on both sides, and financial portfolio prediction with continuous constraints. These examples show how the same layer can support distinct satisfiability formulations. The contribution is a way to build constrained predictions into a neural solver, with demonstrations that do not require expressing the solution process as a sequence of reinforcement learning decisions.
icml-2023-linsatnet-the-positive-linear-.tldr: LinSATNet extends Sinkhorn scaling into a differentiable satisfiability layer for one-shot neural predictions subject to positive linear constraints.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can encourage deep networks to memorize mistakes. The paper focuses on the role of the loss function: cross entropy is unbounded, which contributes to its lack of robustness to noisy labels. Specialized robust losses can address this problem, but the abstract notes that existing designs often introduce underfitting.

LogitClip intervenes in the model’s prediction scores before the loss is evaluated. It caps the norm of the logit vector at a constant, which makes cross entropy effectively bounded. This gives a way to limit the loss through the prediction itself and mitigates overfitting to examples whose labels are noisy.

The authors provide theoretical analyses supporting LogitClip’s noise tolerance. Extensive experiments report substantial improvements in cross entropy’s robustness and broader generalization gains when clipping is combined with popular robust losses. The significance is that the same prediction-level intervention can complement different loss functions, extending its usefulness beyond the particular case of cross entropy without requiring a separate specialized loss for each application.
icml-2023-mitigating-memorization-of-noi.tldr: LogitClip bounds prediction-score norms to curb noisy-label memorization, improving cross entropy and several robust losses in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, a model affects the data it later encounters. This paper studies multiple learning agents connected through two networks. An agent network determines partial cooperation, while a population network determines how an agent’s data depends on its own model and neighboring models. Learning therefore depends on both kinds of connection.

The authors derive sufficient conditions for the existence of performatively stable and Nash equilibria. They also analyze how equilibria change when data distributions are perturbed, obtaining closed-form solutions that explicitly involve network topology. The results connect equilibrium existence to cooperation strength and differences in agents’ responses to structural properties such as node centrality.

A distributed procedure based on stochastic gradient descent is shown to find a performatively stable equilibrium under the stated sufficient condition. Numerical illustrations support the network-effect analysis. The contribution is an account of how cooperation and model-induced changes in data interact, with conditional guarantees for stability and learning rather than a claim that every networked prediction system will converge.
icml-2023-network-effects-in-performativ.tldr: The paper links network structure and cooperation to equilibrium behavior in performative prediction games and proves conditional convergence of distributed SGD.

paragraphs: Local differential privacy protects observations by randomizing them before they are available for analysis. This paper asks how to estimate a population mean and quantify uncertainty using only those privatized values. It considers bounded observations and develops nonparametric, finite-sample inference, so the guarantees do not rely on a large-sample approximation.

The authors generalize randomized response to arbitrary bounded random variables and allow sequential interaction. From the resulting private observations, they construct both confidence intervals for a fixed analysis time and confidence sequences that remain valid across time. The distinction matters when data arrive progressively and uncertainty needs to be tracked throughout collection.

The results include private counterparts of Hoeffding-type bounds for fixed-time and time-uniform inference. The authors also extend the confidence sequences to settings with time-varying means and illustrate private online A/B testing. The contribution combines a privacy mechanism with statistical guarantees for its outputs, making uncertainty assessment possible even when the analyst never sees the original bounded observations.
icml-2023-nonparametric-extensions-of-ra.tldr: Generalized randomized response enables finite-sample confidence intervals and time-uniform confidence sequences for bounded means under local differential privacy.

paragraphs: Offline meta-reinforcement learning uses data from multiple tasks to prepare an agent to adapt quickly. The paper identifies a mismatch that can arise when the agent moves from stored training data to online adaptation: the distribution of transitions and rewards can change. Such adaptation episodes may undermine the reliability of policy evaluation.

The theoretical analysis finds that out-of-distribution episodes can cause unreliable evaluation, while in-distribution episodes can support an adaptation-performance guarantee. Motivated by this result, the authors propose IDAQ, an online adaptation framework using uncertainty quantification. It generates in-distribution context and uses that context to infer which task the agent is facing.

The paper identifies an effective return-based uncertainty measure for IDAQ. On the Meta-World ML1 benchmark, the method achieves the reported state-of-the-art performance against baselines with and without offline adaptation. The findings emphasize the distribution of adaptation experience as a central design issue: useful experience must support reliable evaluation as well as reveal information about the new task.
icml-2023-offline-meta-reinforcement-lea.tldr: IDAQ uses uncertainty to generate in-distribution adaptation context, addressing a theoretically identified distribution shift in offline meta-reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ between individuals, and multiple interacting conditions make those differences difficult to study. This paper develops a graphical framework for representing heterogeneous causal effects. Its motivation includes healthcare problems where both variation among people and the coexistence of disorders complicate causal analysis.

The framework extends causal graphs with multiple mediators and interactions between treatment and confounders. Confounders participating in those interactions act as moderators, allowing the represented effects to vary with their values. The authors derive individual-level forms and properties of heterogeneous effects in both linear and nonlinear models, covering effects from treatment or potential mediators to an outcome.

An interactive structural learning method estimates the graphs and effects and supplies confidence intervals. Extensive simulations support the method empirically, and an application explores causal relationships among psychiatric disorders in trauma survivors. The contribution combines a representation of effect variation, theoretical characterization, and an estimation procedure, allowing heterogeneity to be studied explicitly within a causal graph rather than only through a single overall treatment effect.
icml-2023-on-heterogeneous-treatment-eff.tldr: The paper develops causal graphs and estimation methods that represent individual differences in treatment and mediator effects through moderators and multiple mediators.

paragraphs: CLIP has strong zero-shot image recognition capabilities, and Open-VCLIP adapts that capability to videos. The goal is a video classifier that can recognize actions and events unseen during training. This requires learning relationships across space and time while preserving the broader generalization that makes open-vocabulary recognition useful.

The framework introduces minimal changes to CLIP to model video relationships. The authors formally connect its training problem to continual learning with no historical data. They address that problem with Interpolated Weight Optimization, using weight interpolation during both training and testing to support the transition from an image model to a specialized video classifier.

Evaluation covers three action-recognition datasets under several zero-shot protocols. The paper reports accuracies of 87.9% on UCF, 58.3% on HMDB, and 81.1% on Kinetics-600, outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the combination of video-specific modeling and weight interpolation as a way to adapt pretrained recognition capabilities while retaining useful performance on unseen action categories.
icml-2023-open-vclip-transforming-clip-t.tldr: Open-VCLIP combines minimal video-modeling changes with weight interpolation to adapt CLIP for strong reported zero-shot action recognition.

paragraphs: Class incremental learning introduces new classes over time while requiring a model to retain earlier capabilities. This paper studies the geometry connecting models learned at consecutive stages. It finds that a straight line between adjacent continual-learning minima can cross a high-loss region, making simple interpolation problematic.

The proposed Optimizing Connectivity method searches for a low-loss path around that region using Fourier series and gradient projection. The parameter-saving construction provides a continuous collection of low-loss solutions along the optimized path. The authors then introduce EOPC, which ensembles points within a local bent cylinder to improve performance on previously learned tasks.

The scheme can be added to existing class incremental learning methods. Experiments on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K report consistent improvements when EOPC is combined with representative approaches. The findings give model connectivity a practical role in continual learning: the route between successive solutions can offer useful models for ensembling, beyond what is available from considering the learned endpoints alone.
icml-2023-optimizing-mode-connectivity-f.tldr: OPC finds low-loss paths between successive class-incremental models, and EOPC uses nearby ensembles to improve existing methods in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Phasic Policy Gradient has shown strong sample efficiency and zero-shot generalization on Procgen. Its advantages over PPO were commonly attributed to extensive reuse of value-learning samples and infrequent feature distillation. This paper tests that explanation through an empirical study of which design choices actually sustain the observed performance.

The experiments identify policy regularization and data diversity as the crucial factors in the studied settings. The authors obtain comparable performance with less value-sample reuse and more frequent feature distillation when regularization strength and data diversity are preserved. This separates the effects of the training schedule from other properties that change alongside it.

The study covers all 16 Procgen games in both sample-efficiency and generalization setups. It also shows that PPG’s high performance can be maintained while reducing computation to a level similar to PPO. The findings provide an empirical basis for simplifying PPG and suggest that future designs should pay close attention to regularization and the diversity of training data.
icml-2023-ppg-reloaded-an-empirical-stud.tldr: A Procgen study finds that policy regularization and data diversity sustain PPG’s performance, allowing computational cost to fall to a level similar to PPO.

paragraphs: Laplacian representations encode an environment’s geometry without being tied to a particular reinforcement learning task. Distances between represented states are often used for reward shaping because they are expected to reflect reachability. The paper shows that this expectation need not hold: nearby points in the representation can correspond to states that are far apart in the environment.

The proposed Reachability-Aware Laplacian Representation rescales each dimension of the original representation. This directly changes how distances are computed without abandoning the Laplacian representation itself. The aim is to make closeness in the learned space better reflect how reachable one state is from another.

The authors provide theoretical explanations and experimental evidence that the rescaled representation captures reachability better. They also report a substantial improvement in reward shaping and benefits for discovering bottleneck states. The contribution links a specific geometric mismatch to downstream learning behavior and shows that correcting the relative scales of representation dimensions can improve the usefulness of distance-based guidance.
icml-2023-reachability-aware-laplacian-r.tldr: Rescaling Laplacian representation dimensions better aligns distances with state reachability, improving reward shaping and bottleneck discovery in the reported results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a single neuron when labels may contain adversarial noise. It evaluates predictions with squared error, so the goal is to find a neuron whose error is close to the best achievable error despite corrupted supervision. The activation functions covered include ReLUs and a broader family.

The authors give an efficient algorithm with a constant-factor approximation guarantee for the optimal squared error. This means the result controls error relative to the best attainable value; it does not require the noisy learning problem to have a zero-error solution. The guarantee concerns the studied single-neuron setting.

The key technical ingredient connects the learning problem to local error bounds from optimization theory. This connection allows the algorithm to work under substantially milder distributional assumptions than earlier work. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and analytical: it provides an efficient robust-learning procedure and identifies optimization structure that supports guarantees across a broader range of data distributions.
icml-2023-robustly-learning-a-single-neu.tldr: An efficient algorithm learns a single neuron under adversarial label noise with a constant-factor squared-error guarantee and milder distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: Large sets may need to be processed in chunks, but their representation should not depend on how those chunks are chosen. Mini-batch consistency formalizes that requirement: partitioning and aggregating the same set must give the same output. Existing architectures enforcing it can restrict expressive power, and training creates a separate challenge when full-set gradients are needed.

The paper introduces Universally Mini-Batch Consistent set functions that can be combined with arbitrary non-consistent components while preserving the framework’s consistency property. This expands the function classes available for set encoding. It also proposes a training algorithm that gives an unbiased approximation of the full-set gradient.

The algorithm has constant memory overhead with respect to set size during training and testing. Experiments cover image completion, text classification, unsupervised clustering, and cancer detection in high-resolution images, supporting the framework’s efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution addresses both representation design and training scalability, so processing a set in chunks need not force the same architectural restrictions or require storing a full-set gradient computation.
icml-2023-scalable-set-encoding-with-uni.tldr: UMBC expands expressive set encoding while preserving partition consistency and supplies unbiased full-set gradient approximation with constant memory overhead.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent may receive incomplete or noisy observations instead of directly seeing the environment’s true state. This paper studies decision-making under that uncertainty using sets of possible hidden states. Its motivation is that probability estimates alone may not provide the definite belief regions useful for reliable decisions.

Set-membership Belief state-based Reinforcement Learning combines two parts. A belief-state learning model estimates bounded sets of possible states, and a reinforcement learning controller makes decisions using those sets. The central theoretical result shows that the estimated sets always contain the true states under unknown-but-bounded noise.

The bounded-noise condition is essential to the stated containment guarantee: uncertainty is unknown in detail but constrained in magnitude. Benchmark experiments support the method’s effectiveness and report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution connects a set-based representation of uncertainty with control, giving the controller belief regions supported by a containment result in the studied noise setting.
icml-2023-set-membership-belief-state-ba.tldr: SBRL controls partially observed systems using learned belief sets that provably contain the true state under unknown-but-bounded noise.

paragraphs: Whether an object fits somewhere can depend on just a few dimensions, such as its height beneath a shelf or its width through a doorway. The paper calls these crucial quantities geometric eigen-lengths. It asks whether a learning system can discover such compact, interpretable object descriptions through experience with fitting tasks.

The authors formulate this as a learning problem and build a benchmark suite containing tasks, data, and evaluation metrics. They explore candidate solutions and show that learning eigen-lengths is feasible from observations of successful and unsuccessful fitting trials. This makes task outcomes the evidence from which useful geometric quantities are learned.

The study also attempts geometric grounding to improve measurement accuracy and examines whether learned eigen-lengths can be reused across multiple tasks. Its findings establish an exploratory starting point rather than a complete general solution. The broader contribution is to make the discovery of a few task-relevant geometric measurements an explicit learning objective, with a benchmark for investigating how those measurements emerge and transfer.
icml-2023-towards-learning-geometric-eig.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and shows the feasibility of learning crucial object dimensions from successful and failed fitting trials.
